activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Rosa's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Uncle Sam held a plate of pizza bites. Mrs. Rosa said, "Watch this part!"

Then the TV picture went frozen. It just stopped. The players stood like statues. "Oh no," said Uncle Sam. "Not now!"

Leon wanted to see the goal. He looked all around. Then he saw something. The dog, Biscuit, had a string from the curtain in his mouth. Biscuit pulled the string. The string was tied to the little black box behind the TV. When Biscuit pulled, the picture wobbled!

"Biscuit, drop it!" said Leon. Biscuit dropped the string and wagged his tail.

Mr. Rosa knelt down and fixed the little black box. "All safe now," he said. "You have sharp eyes, Leon." The picture moved again. The players ran!

Uncle Sam took a big bite of his pizza bite and cheered. "Go, go, go!" he shouted.

Biscuit jumped on the couch next to Leon. Leon held the curtain string up high, far from the dog. "This is my job," Leon said. "You watch the game."

Biscuit licked his nose just as the crowd on TV shouted, "Goal!"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Daniel put on his little white hat. He was baking bread for his family. "I will make the biggest bread ever," he said.

He mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Then he added more and more flour. The spoon got stuck. The dough was stiff like a rock. "Oh no," said Daniel. "My dough will not move."

His teacher laughed softly. "Try a splash of water," she said. Daniel poured in a splash. He mixed. The water made the dough soft and squishy. "It moves again," he shouted. He squished it with his hands. It felt like play dough.

The teacher put the pan in the hot oven. Daniel stayed at the safe table and helped clean the big bowl. Soon the bread came out, big and golden.

At home, everyone ate it up. "More bread, Daniel," said Dad. Daniel grinned and said, "I will need a bigger bowl."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Wesley stood in the band room. He held a big drum. He wanted to make it boom.

"Hit it hard," said Miss Kay. Wesley swung his arm. He hit the drum. It made a tiny sound. Tap. That was all.

Wesley frowned. He wanted a big boom. He tried again. Tap. Tap. Too small!

Then he looked at his drumstick. The soft round end was hitting the drum. He turned the stick around. Now the hard little end was down.

He swung his arm. He hit the drum. BOOM! The drum went boom so big, it made a cymbal wobble on the shelf. The cymbal fell over with a crunchy crash.

"Oops," said Wesley.

Miss Kay laughed. "Big boom," she said. "Maybe not that big."

Wesley hit the drum again. Boom. Boom. Boom. Just right. Then he played a song for his mom at pick-up time. She clapped very loud.

"Play the boom part again," she said. Wesley grinned and swung his arm.

story:

She had cut a square for the house. She had cut a triangle for the roof. "Cutting makes shapes," said Mia. John got the safe paper and the kid scissors. He cut a square. He cut a triangle too. He cut a small rectangle for the door. Then he cut a circle for the sun. He glued them all on.

Miss Amy held the glue gun. "Only I use this," she said. "It can burn your finger." John watched from his seat. The hot glue held the roof on tight. He pressed the paper shapes with his clean hand. Then he drew curly lines by the door. "Look, curly smoke from my chimney!" said John. Mia smiled and gave him a yellow crayon. John drew rays all around his circle sun. "A square, a triangle, a rectangle, and a circle," he said. "My house is done!" Miss Amy hung it on the wall, up high where everyone could see.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Myles ran into the sunny backyard. The sun warmed his back. He took off his big coat. "Too hot!" he said.

Then the wind began to whoosh. The wind lifted his hat right off his head. The naughty wind sent the hat under the bush. "Come back, hat!" Myles called.

Dark clouds rolled in. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. The rain made little ponds on the stones. Myles put his hat back on and pulled up his hood. Now the rain could not wet his hair.

In winter, snow would fall here. Snow could freeze the pond hard. Myles would wear mittens and boots.

A little turtle sat by the pond. It did not mind the rain at all. "Do you like the rain, turtle?" Myles asked. The turtle slid slowly into the water.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Camille wanted warm milk before her nap. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Camille stayed right by the table.

Grandma turned on the stove. Blue flames jumped up. Camille saw the pot. Steam rose from the pot like little clouds. Grandma held up her hand near the steam. "Hot," she said softly. Camille held up her hand far away. She did not feel hot. Far was safe.

Camille counted the safe things she could touch. "One, the cup. Two, the spoon. Three, my napkin." Grandma poured the warm milk. She poured and poured, until the cup began to fill. Camille wrapped both hands around the cup. Warm, not hot. Just right.

Camille sipped her milk. It tasted like a sweet dream. "I was brave," she whispered. Grandma kissed the top of her head. Camille counted again. "One, warm cup. Two, soft kiss. Three, sleepy girl."

story:

Next she heard a buzz. A yellow bee flew to a flower. The flower was yellow too. "I see yellow," said Madison. But the bee flew away fast. Madison looked down and found yellow pollen on her finger. She wiped it into the jar.

Then she saw green grass and picked one blade. She saw blue sky and shut the lid tight. "Now my jar has the sky," she said. She held the jar up high. The colors mixed in the sun and glowed. A little snake slid by and looked up. Madison waved. "Hello, snake. Want to see my rainbow?"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Sophie sat in the family car. She buckled her seat belt all by herself. Today was a big day. They were going to get the new baby.

"Who is in our family?" asked Daddy.

"Mama, Daddy, me," said Sophie. She held up one finger, two fingers, three.

"Now there will be four," said Daddy.

The baby was small and light as a loaf of bread. Daddy carried him out and put his seat in the car. Then the baby began to cry. He cried loud and long. Sophie covered her ears. She wanted the baby to like the car. She wanted him to stop.

Sophie had an idea. She took her deep blue blanket from her bag. She could not reach the baby. But she could reach her own teddy. She held teddy up so the baby could see it. She sang her quiet song, the one Mama sang at night. "Sleep, baby, sleep," she sang.

The baby looked at teddy. The crying got small. Then the crying stopped. The baby made a soft sound and closed his eyes. He fell asleep because of her song. Sophie had made that happen.

"Who is in our family?" asked Mama, smiling in the mirror.

"Mama, Daddy, me, and baby," said Sophie. One finger, two fingers, three fingers, four. When they got home, they would sit together on the couch. Mama had cookies waiting, one for Sophie and one for Daddy, and the baby would sleep in his blanket.

"Good work, big sister," said Daddy.

Sophie sang her quiet song all the way home.

story:
Benjamin wanted to play house at daycare. But the baby doll was missing. "Where is Baby?" he asked. Mia pointed at the big toy box. Benjamin dug deep. He pushed teddy bears aside. Then he found the doll, all wrapped in a sock.

The sock was Baby's blanket. Benjamin rocked Baby in his arms. "Time to eat," he said. He gave Baby a wooden bowl. Mia was the cook. "Soup is ready," she called. The soup was just green blocks in a cup.

Benjamin fed Baby one spoonful. Baby fell over. Benjamin gasped. "Baby is scared of the spoon!" he said. He tipped the bowl to Baby's mouth instead. Baby stayed sitting up. "Baby likes the bowl better," Benjamin laughed.

Then Mia built a mountain of pillows. Baby slid down the mountain. Whee! Benjamin clapped and picked Baby up. "Again, again!" said Mia, pushing the pillows higher.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Aurora ran into Grandma's kitchen. The whole family was coming today. There were big breads on the table and cups of juice.

"Can we eat now?" Aurora asked.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "First we hold hands. Then someone says the special words."

Aurora wanted to say the words. She asked, "Can it be me?"

"You need to learn them first," said Grandma.

Grandma said the words slow. Aurora tried to hurry. She mixed them all up. Everyone laughed, but it was a nice laugh.

Then Aurora had an idea. She found a pencil. Daddy wrote the words on a card. Aurora drew a sun on it too.

Everyone sat down at the big table. They all held hands. Aurora stood up tall. She looked at her card.

"Thank you for our food and our family," she said. "Bless everyone here."

Everyone smiled at once. Then everyone picked up their bread at the same time. Grandpa winked at her.

"You did it!" said Mommy. "Now we can eat."

Aurora bit into her warm bread. She was a lucky girl.

"Can I do it again tomorrow?" she asked.

Grandma squeezed her hand and said, "Yes, every day."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Violet put on her special dress. Her family was going to a big house of prayer. Today there was a festival with songs and food.

Violet wanted to see the lamps. There were many little lamps at the front. They looked like tiny stars. But the lamps were far away, and she was small. The tall people stood all around her. She could not see anything but coats and sleeves.

Mama knelt down beside her. "You can sit on the step," Mama said. It was a wide stone step. Violet climbed up all by herself. Now she was taller. She could see the whole row of lamps. Each little flame stood up straight and warm. Grandma lit one more lamp with a long match. The new flame came up, and then a new smell of sweet smoke floated over.

"Do you see it, Violet?" Grandma asked.

"Yes," said Violet. She planted her hands on her knees and watched. One flame. Then sweet smoke. Again and again, like magic that was not scary at all.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Violet ran to school. She was almost late. She had eaten her breakfast fast.

In the music room, Miss Ana sat at the piano. "Let's sing our counting song," she said. Violet loved that song. "One, two, three, four, five," they all sang. Then they sang more. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Then Miss Ana dropped the rhythm sticks. The sticks rolled under the shelf. Ten little sticks rolled far, far away.

"Can you help, Violet?" asked Miss Ana. Violet got down on her knees. She reached under the shelf. She pulled the sticks out one at a time. "One," said Violet. She pulled again. "Two." She kept pulling. "Three, four, five."

Miss Ana put each stick back in the box. Violet pulled out more. "Six, seven, eight, nine." One stick was still hiding. Violet reached way in. Her fingers found it. "Ten!" she said.

Miss Ana closed the box. All the sticks fit just right. "You found them all," said Miss Ana. "Now we can play the song." The sticks tapped one, two, three, four, five. They tapped six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

Violet smiled and tapped along. "Again, again!" she said.

story:
Clara wanted to help at school. She wanted to make snack time come fast. Her teacher, Miss Rose, said, "First we wait for the bread."

Clara looked at the big oven. Miss Rose put the bread in. "It is hot," said Miss Rose. "You stay way back here." Clara stood back. The oven was hot. Her juice box was cold. She held it in her hands.

A little bird landed at the window. It had one wing up, then both wings out. It was small. Clara was big next to it. The bird flapped fast. Clara waved slow. The bird came closer. Then it flew away. "Come back, little bird," said Clara.

She waited and waited. Miss Rose took the bread out. It smelled good. Miss Rose cut it, one, two, three. The bread steamed. Clara blew on her piece. She blew slow. The steam went away. Now the bread was just warm. Clara took a bite. "Yum," she said. "The little bird missed this."

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
William was at summer camp. There was one big red truck on the toy shelf. William wanted that truck more than anything.

Ben grabbed the truck first. William grabbed it too. The truck went squeak, squeak. Both boys pulled. Then the wheel fell off. It rolled under the table.

William got down on his knees. He reached for the wheel. He pushed it back on. The wheel made the truck roll again. William held the truck out to Ben. "Your turn first," he said.

Ben drove the truck in a circle. "Your turn now," said Ben. William took the truck and drove it to the sandbox. The sand felt warm on his toes.

Then William filled a bowl with sand. He tipped it over. The sand made a round, friendly hill. Ben laughed and clapped. "Make another one," said Ben. So William filled the bowl again, and Ben waited, with his hands in his lap, until it was his turn.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. It was cold outside. Rehmat wanted to wear her red coat all by herself.

She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat sat crooked on her shoulders. One sleeve hung down empty. "Silly sleeve," said Rehmat. The sleeve flapped like a wing when she moved.

Mama smiled. Rehmat tried again. Arm in, arm in, and pull. The coat sat straight now. Time for the zipper. Rehmat pulled it up, but the zipper slid back down. She frowned at it.

Then Rehmat looked down. The two sides of her coat were apart. She pushed them together at the bottom. She pulled the zipper again. Zip! It went all the way up to her chin. "I did it!" said Rehmat. Mama clapped.

The bank man gave Rehmat a red apple for being so patient. Rehmat held it with her warm hands. "My coat is on, and it will not come off," she said. She marched to the door, and the zipper gleamed in the light.

story:
Luka sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint a sun, but there was no orange paint. He looked in the cup. Only red, yellow and blue.

Luka felt shy about asking. He watched the red paint. He watched the yellow paint. Then he tried something. He dipped his brush in red. He made a red dot on the paper. He dipped the brush in yellow. He put yellow right on the red dot.

The two colours touched. They moved together. The dot turned orange! Luka blinked. He made another dot. Red, then yellow. Orange again.

"Look, Mother," he said at pick-up time. He held up his orange sun. His mother smiled big. "That sun looks warm," she said. Luka touched the wet paper with one finger. His fingerprint came out orange too.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Joshua ran into the cooking classroom. Today he would make muffins for his whole family. "Blueberry muffins for Mama, Daddy, and Baby Ruth!" he said. "One, two, three muffins, and one for me. Four!"

He put flour in the big bowl. He cracked an egg. He poured in milk. Then he began to stir. Round and round went the spoon. The batter was thick and lumpy, like mud. "Silly, naughty lumps," said Joshua. "Go away!" He stirred and stirred. The lumps went away. Now the batter was smooth and shiny.

But wait. Joshua had forgotten the blueberries! He dropped them in. He stirred again. The white batter turned purple, purple, purple. Joshua laughed. "The blueberries make it purple!"

Miss Amy put the pan in the hot oven. Joshua watched from far away. Soon a yummy smell filled the room. Then the timer rang. Out came four big muffins, warm and blue.

Joshua carried them home in a basket. "Muffins!" said Mama. "For you, and you, and you," said Joshua. Baby Ruth clapped her hands. Joshua took a big bite. "Purple inside!" he said.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red ball in the toy box. The ball was bumpy all over. Charlie wanted to hold it.

A boy named Ben had the ball first. Charlie ran over fast. She reached out to grab it.

Her grandma put a hand on her arm. "Let's wait," Grandma said softly. Charlie sat on her leg and folded her hands. It was hard to wait. She watched Ben roll the bumpy ball on the floor.

Then Ben rolled the ball right to her. "Your turn," he said. Charlie caught it. It felt funny in her hands, like tiny bumps on her skin.

Ben sat down to wait, just like Charlie did. A bug crawled near his shoe, and he stopped to scratch his leg. While he scratched, Charlie rolled the ball back to him.

Ben laughed and rolled it again. "We can both play," he said.

Charlie clapped her hands. The party had cake next. Grandma held the candle, and everyone sang. Ben sat right next to Charlie.

"Best party," said Charlie, holding the bumpy ball in her lap.

Miles sat in the car with his blanket. They were going to the salon for his first haircut. "I want my hair to stay," said Miles.

At the salon, the hairdresser put a cape on him. She sprayed his hair with water. Miles felt the wet drops. "Cold!" he said. The hairdresser laughed kindly. Then she began to snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the cape like tiny dark snow.

Miles watched one piece fall on his arm. He blew on it. The hair jumped up and slid away. He blew again. Another piece slid off. "Look, Mom!" said Miles. He kept blowing, and the hairs kept sliding. When it was done, Miles marched to the car. His hair was short and soft. He touched it all the way home.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday Parker painted a picture at school. It was a gift for his mom. But paint takes time to dry. His paper was still wet at home time.

Today Parker looked for his picture on the shelf. It was missing! "Where did it go?" he asked. His teacher said, "Let's look for it." They looked in the paint corner. They looked by the window. The sun was shining there.

There it was! The warm sun had touched the wet paint all night. Now the paper was dry and flat. Parker touched it with one finger. "All dry," he said. "Now it can be a gift."

"Can I take it home now?" he asked.

"Yes," said his teacher. "Take it now."

Parker held it all the way to the car.

Anna lost her bunny at school. She looked and looked. "Where is bunny?" she said.

Anna looked by the slide. No bunny. She looked by the swings. No bunny. Then the wind blew. The wind lifted a short red scarf on the ground. Under the scarf was bunny!

"Bunny! I found you!" said Anna. She gave bunny a big hug.

The wind blew again. It lifted the scarf up high. Anna laughed. She watched the wind fold the scarf right back down.

"Time to go," said Mama. Anna held bunny close. They walked past the park gate together.

"Goodbye, wind," said Anna. "Thank you for showing me bunny." The scarf fluttered softly, like a little wave goodbye.

Milo went to the park with his dad. He saw a hoop on the grass. Dad held out a beanbag. "Throw it in," said Dad.

Milo threw it. The beanbag went low. It hit the rim and fell out. Milo got the beanbag. He stood very close to the hoop. He threw it high. The beanbag went up and then down. It fell in! "It went in!" said Milo. Dad clapped.

Then Dad rolled a big ball to Milo. Milo held out one hand. The ball hit his hand and fell. Milo sat down in the grass. He felt dizzy from turning to chase it. Dad came close. activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eli sat on the little red mat at daycare. Miss Ana held up a book. "This book is from the library," she said. "We can take it home, but we must bring it back."

Eli loved the book about the big red truck. He read it with Miss Ana. She opened the top page first. She turned each page one by one. The words on the page told her what to say. The words said, "The truck goes fast!"

"No," said Miss Ana. "Someone else wants to read it too. But you can borrow it again."

Eili frowned. Then he had an idea. "Can I hold it one more time?"

"You can," said Miss Ana.

Eli held the book. He turned the pages, front to back. He pointed at the words. "Truck!" he said.

Tomorrow, his friend Mia would read it. And after that, Eli would borrow it again.

"Fast truck," said Eli, and he turned to the top page one more time.

Mama poured the batter. Bubbles popped up, pop, pop, pop. "Flip it now," said Mama. The pancacake turned golden. Lena wore her fox apron. The fox had a happy face, just like Lena.

story:
Henry got in the family car. They were going on a big trip to Grandma's house. Henry had his own little bag. Inside were his teddy bear, his blocks, and one shoe.

Dad looked at the bag. "It is too full," said Dad. "The zipper will not close."

Henry tried to pull the zipper. It would not move. The bag was stuffed like a big round ball.

"Why will it not close?" Henry asked.

"Too many things are inside," said Dad.

Henry looked in his bag. He took out one block. He tried the zipper again. Still stuck! He took out the shoe. Now the bag was soft and squishy. Henry pulled the zipper. Zip! It closed all the way.

"My bag closed!" Henry shouted.

Dad put the bag in the car. Then they drove off. The sky got dark and stormy on the way. Henry held his teddy tight. Soon they would see Grandma's front door.

"Are we almost there?" Henry asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Look out the window."

Henry saw Grandma waving by her gate.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Ibrahim wanted to dress his robot. But the robot had no clothes at all.

Ibrahim looked out the big window. The sun was shining. "It is sunny," he said. He put a little hat on the robot's head. Sun hats are good for sunny days.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell, drip drip. "It is rainy," said Ibrahim. He put little boots on the robot. Rain boots are good for rainy days.

The wind blew hard. "It is windy!" said Ibrahim. The wind pushed the hat right off. He held the hat and put it back on. Then he remembered the coat. He wrapped a tiny coat around the robot.

Mama came to the window. "What about snow?" she asked. She opened her hand. A white mitten fell out, soft as snow. "A surprise for your robot," she said.

Ibrahim put the mitten on the robot's hand. "Now you are ready," he said. He hugged the robot tight. Outside, the rain went drip, drip, drip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Evelyn wanted to sing the whole song. But she forgot the words in the middle. Mommy sang "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Evelyn sang "Twinkle" and then stopped. She frowned.

Mommy clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Try clapping with me," said Mommy. Evelyn watched Mommy's hands. They went up and down like a little bird. Evelyn clapped too. Her claps were fast, fast, fast. "Too speedy," laughed Mommy. "Slow your hands down." Evelyn watched the red block on the floor. It sat still. She thought of slow, still things.

Evelyn made her hands go slow. Clap, clap, clap. The claps matched Mommy's song. Then the words came out too. "How I wonder what you are." She did not stop. She sang it all the way to the end. Baby brother woke up from his nap and cried. Evelyn clapped slow claps and sang again, soft this time. Baby stopped crying. He watched her hands go up and down.

"Again," said Evelyn. "Up above the world so high." Baby kicked his feet and made a happy sound.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Kinsley ran to the swings at the park. The big swing was wet from the rain. "Slippery," said Mama. Kinsley touched it. Her hands slid down. She wanted to swing so much.

Kinsley saw a boy on the dry swing next to her. "Can you please help me get a dry swing?" she asked Mama. "Yes," said Mama. She wiped the wet swing with a towel. "Thank you," said Kinsley. She climbed up. The swing was dry now. She pumped her legs. Up she went!

Then the boy fell off his swing. He sat on the ground. "Sorry," said Kinsley. "Are you okay?" The boy nodded. His dad came fast and picked him up. Kinsley kept swinging. Mama waved from the bench. Kinsley waved back, way up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Paisley had a new pet. It was a small orange fish. His name was Pip.

Pip swam in his bowl by the window. Paisley wanted to touch him. She tapped on the glass. Tap, tap. Pip hid behind the little green plant. He did not come out.

"Poor Pip," said Mama. "Watch and see." Mama did not tap. She sat very still. Soon Pip peeked out. Then he swam in a big slow circle.

Paisley tried too. She sat very still, just like Mama. Her hands stayed in her lap. Pip came out of the plant. He blew a tiny bubble.

Paisley fed Pip one small pinch of food. The flakes looked like yummy little stars to her, but they were fish food. Pip gobbled them up.

Outside, the moon came up. It was big and round. The moonlight shone on the fish bowl. Pip swam past the light and back again.

Paisley did not tap on the glass anymore. She just sat and watched. Pip swam right up close to her. He waved his little fin.

"Night night, Pip," said Paisley.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Georgia put on her big sun hat. The hat was too loose. It fell over her eyes. "I can't see!" she said. Papa laughed softly. "Then push it up."

Georgia pushed up the hat. Now she could see the farm. She saw a red barn. She saw a fluffy white sheep. "My eyes see the sheep!" she said.

Papa gave her a soft piece of hay. Georgia touched it with her fingers. "My hands feel the hay. It is prickly." Then the sheep went "Baa!" Georgia giggled. "My ears hear the sheep." A warm breeze came by. It smelled like apples. "My nose smells apples," Georgia said.

They walked to the apple tree. Papa picked a small red apple. He washed it and cut it with his knife. Georgia waited. Then she took a little bite. "Yum! My mouth tastes the apple!" Papa smiled. "You found all five," he said. Georgia clapped her hands. Her hat slipped down again. She pushed it up and laughed. "Eyes again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Olivia's class was going outside. Teacher Sam said, "Coats on!" Everyone ran to the hooks. Olivia grabbed her purple coat.

She pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat hung behind her, funny and low. Teacher Sam said, "You can fix it. Take your time."

Olivia looked at the tag inside the collar. The tag was by her knees. She wiggled the coat off. She turned it around. Now the tag was at her neck. She pushed her arms in again. This time the coat sat just right on her back.

Next came the zipper. Olivia held the bottom part. She pushed the zipper down into it. Click. It caught! She pulled the slider up, up, up. The coat closed all the way to her chin.

Teacher Sam looked at the clock. "Still time before outside," he said. Olivia smiled and pulled the zipper down, then up again, just to see it open and close.

"Look at me!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Axel sat down at the dinner table. He saw a big bowl of green peas. "I want peas!" he said. Mama said, "Let's count them first."

Axel clapped his hands. Mama put peas on his plate. "One, two, three," she said. Axel tapped each pea with his spoon. "Four, five, six!" he said. The peas rolled a little. He laughed.

Then Axel saw one pea near the edge. He pushed it with his finger. It rolled right off the plate. It dropped under the table. "Oh no!" said Axel. "My pea is missing!"

Papa bent down and looked. "I see it," he said. He picked it up. "Let's not forget this little pea." Axel giggled. Papa put it back on the plate.

"Now count again," said Mama. Axel pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" He counted so fast. Then he ate one pea. "Now six!" he shouted.

Papa said, "Count to ten and eat them all." Axel grinned. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then he opened his mouth wide. "Yum, yum, yum," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milan wanted to plant a seed at school. Yesterday, his teacher had shown the class a bean. She said they would plant it today. Today was now. Milan held his little pot.

"Can we plant it now?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Ada. "Now we will put the bean in the dirt. Later, we will give it water. Tomorrow, it might look different."

Milan pushed the bean into the dark dirt. He patted it down, pat, pat, pat. Then he waited his turn for the watering can. He poured the water, drop by drop. The dirt turned dark and wet.

"Where is my plant?" he asked.

"Tomorrow," said Miss Ada. "You must wait."

Milan put the pot on the bright windowsill. He looked at it all day. At story time, he looked again. The pot sat still.

The next day, Milan ran to the window. He leaned in close. A tiny green tip was poking out of the dirt. "It came!" he shouted. "The bean grew in the night!"

Miss Ada smiled and gave him a shiny coin sticker for his pot. "Look what waiting can do," she said.

Milan tapped the glass. "Grow more tomorrow," he whispered to the little green tip. "I will come back and see you."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson woke up in his soft bed. The sun made a warm spot on his blanket. He rubbed his eyes and called, "Mama, I'm up!"

First came breakfast. Jaxson ate one egg, one piece of toast, and one banana. He counted them on his plate. "One, two, three," he said. His tummy felt happy and full. The banana tasted sweet on his tongue.

Then Jaxson played in the sandbox outside. His sister, a big girl named Mia, played too. They dug and patted and poured. Soon Jaxson's hands were dirty. His feet were dirty. Even his nose had a smudge of dirt. "Time for a bath," said Mama. She filled the tub with warm water. Jaxson stepped in carefully. The water turned brown and cloudy. "Look, Mama! The dirt left my feet!" Mama smiled and let the dirty water go down the drain. Jaxson came out clean and pink.

He put on one shirt, one sock, one sock, and one cozy sleeper. He counted again. Then he found a surprise under his pillow. It was his little rubber duck, hiding there all day. "Quack," said Jaxson. Mama laughed and kissed his head. Jaxson hugged the duck and closed his sleepy eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zoe packed her little red bag. "We go on a trip today!" said Mama. They drove a long, long way to the big park.

At the park, Daddy set up the tent. Zoe wanted her teddy bear. She looked in the car. She looked by the tree. No teddy. Zoe's lip went wobbly.

"Let's open your bag and look," said Mama. Zoe unzipped the bag. There was teddy, under her socks! Zoe had packed him herself. She hugged him tight.

Later, they walked on a bumpy path. Zoe saw a wheel on Daddy's cart. Daddy pulled the cart, and the wheel turned. When the wheel turned, the cart rolled. When Daddy stopped, the wheel stopped too. Zoe laughed and patted the wheel.

At night, Daddy made a fire far away. Zoe sat with Mama on the big log. An owl made a sound, "Who, who." Zoe held teddy close.

"It's just an owl," said Mama. "We are all here together."

Zoe yawned. She snuggled into her warm sleeping bag. "Night night, teddy," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Billie stood in the kitchen. Her mom was cooking soup on the stove. Billie held her mom's leg and stayed close. The pot made steam. The steam went up, up, up.

"Is the soup hot?" Billie asked.

"Yes, very hot," said Mom. "Only I touch the pot."

Billie touched a spoon on the counter. The spoon was cold. The spoon did not make steam. The pot was hot, and the pot made steam. So Billie could tell which one was which.

"I need to stir," said Mom. "You can sit on your swing outside."

The sun was bright in the yard. Billie sat on her swing. Through the window, she watched Mom stir the hot soup. She swung her legs and waited for lunch.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Hayden wanted to wash his toy lion. The lion had jam on its mane. Hayden held the lion in the bathroom. He reached for the shiny tap.

Mama put her hand over his. "Let me do the tap," she said. Mama turned it a little. The water ran warm, not hot. Hayden put his fingers in. It felt nice. He put the lion's paw in too. The jam began to melt away.

Then Hayden saw the little bottle by the sink. He reached for it. "That one is for grown-ups," said Mama. She moved it up high. Hayden looked at his lion instead. He rubbed the mane with a soft cloth. Round and round he went. The jam came off. The lion was clean and special again. Hayden gave the lion a big hug. "All done," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Aaron lost his blue toy car. He loved that car. He looked for it at school, on the big playground.

"Where is my car?" said Aaron. His friend Mia came to help. "Let's look by the slide," she said. They looked there. No car. They looked by the swings. No car. The sky was cloudy, and everything looked gray.

Then the sun came out. The clouds moved away. The slide got bright. The sandbox got bright too. Something in the sandbox shined. It was a little blue shine! Aaron ran to the sandbox. He dug in the sand with his hands. Out came his blue car!

"The sun helped me find it," said Aaron. "The light made it shine!"

Mia clapped. "Good looking, Aaron!"

"Want to make it ride down the slide?" said Aaron. "Yes!" said Mia. The little blue car zoomed down, and the two friends laughed.
